<reason>A (CON) won the decisive definitional clash: the motion names a specific charter — securities classification as admission ticket plus issuer registration/disclosure — and B never defended that machinery on the assets that matter. B conceded issuer-less assets get "nothing" from the charter's signature tool, routed BTC/ETH (most volume) to a commodities affiliate, and left A's SIPC asset-gating point unanswered, leaving B defending the word "securities" rather than the charter. B's main counter — that any regime with segregation, capital, and exams "is" the broker-dealer position, so A abandoned "lightly supervised" — was a real textual hit but proved too much: it dissolves the motion's "rather than," and A showed those protections are generic intermediary tools found in commodities and payments regimes, not charter-exclusive. A's empirical work (Madoff exams missing the fraud, the FTX affiliate being commodities-regulated) was accurate and damaging; B's closing leaned on a mischaracterized version of the FTX affiliate that A had already corrected on the record. B was rhetorically excellent and candid under pressure, keeping this competitive; A's clipped Rebuttal 2 was a minor execution cost but left no burden unanswered.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The FTX-affiliate exchange: A introduced that FTX's CFTC-regulated derivatives affiliate kept customer funds segregated and solvent while the offshore exchange commingled — turning B's best failure example into live proof that modular, non-securities regulation does the protecting. B's attempted flip ("the affiliate regulated like a broker... the label lost") misdescribed a commodities-regulated entity as vindicating the securities charter, and A's on-record correction ("commodity-regulated segregation, not the charter") neutralized what became the centerpiece of B's closing.</best_rebuttal>
